title: Secret Management
summary: Secrets — database passwords, API tokens, TLS certificates — must never be committed to Git or hardcoded in images. The DevOps ecosystem has several solutions: Kubernetes Secrets (baseline), External Secrets Operator (syncs from a secret store), HashiCorp Vault (full secret management), and Sealed Secrets (encrypted secrets in Git). The sandbox demonstrates External Secrets Operator.

sections.title: The secrets problem: why plaintext fails
sections.body:
Secrets are the most common source of production security incidents. Understanding why each approach fails sets up the solution.

**The anti-patterns:**

```bash norun
# ✗ Hardcoded in source code
DB_PASSWORD = "<CHANGE_ME>"     # visible to anyone with repo access

# ✗ In .env files committed to Git
echo 'DB_PASSWORD=<CHANGE_ME>' >> .env
git add .env && git commit -m "add config"  # now it's in git history forever

# ✗ In Docker images (docker history exposes them)
FROM python:3.12
ENV DB_PASSWORD=<CHANGE_ME>     # visible in image layers

# ✗ In Kubernetes manifests checked into Git
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  password: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=  # base64 is NOT encryption!
```

**What base64 is not:**

```bash
# base64 is encoding, not encryption
echo '<CHANGE_ME>' | base64
# c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=

# Trivially reversed:
echo 'c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=' | base64 -d
# <CHANGE_ME>

# Kubernetes Secrets are base64 in etcd by default
# Anyone with kubectl access to the Secret can decode it
# Enable etcd encryption at rest for real protection
```

**Secret rotation problem:**

```
When credentials are hardcoded, rotation means:
1. Update every place the secret is hardcoded
2. Redeploy all services that use it
3. Hope you didn't miss any

With a secret manager:
1. Rotate in the secret manager
2. Applications automatically pick up the new value
   (via environment injection or secret reload)
```

**The CIA triad applied to secrets:**

```
Confidentiality — only authorized services/users can read the secret
               (RBAC, access policies, audit logs)

Integrity      — secrets cannot be tampered with undetected
               (audit trail, versioning, signing)

Availability   — services can always fetch their secrets
               (HA secret store, caching, fallback mechanisms)
```

sections.title: Kubernetes Secrets: the baseline
sections.body:
Kubernetes Secrets are the native secret mechanism. They're required for many K8s features (TLS, image pull credentials) and are the target format for all secret management tools.

```bash
# Create secrets imperatively
kubectl create secret generic db-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=appuser \
  --from-literal=password=<CHANGE_ME>

# kubectl create secret generic tls-certs \
#   --from-file=tls.crt=./server.crt \
#   --from-file=tls.key=./server.key   # (requires actual cert files)

# Create a Docker registry secret (image pull)
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=myuser \
  --docker-password=<YOUR_REGISTRY_TOKEN>

# View secrets (base64 encoded)
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o yaml

# Decode a specific field
kubectl get secret db-credentials \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
```

**Consuming secrets in pods:**

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1

    # Method 1: environment variables from secret
    env:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password

    # Method 2: inject all keys as env vars
    envFrom:
    - secretRef:
        name: db-credentials

    # Method 3: mount as files
    volumeMounts:
    - name: certs
      mountPath: /etc/certs
      readOnly: true

  volumes:
  - name: certs
    secret:
      secretName: tls-certs
```

**RBAC for secrets:**

```yaml
# Restrict secret access — only the app SA can read its secret
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: secret-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  resourceNames: ["db-credentials"]  # only THIS secret
  verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: app-reads-secret
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app
  namespace: production
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: secret-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**Limitations of native Kubernetes Secrets:**

```
✗ Not encrypted in etcd by default
✗ Still stored in Kubernetes (what if cluster is compromised?)
✗ No rotation — secrets don't auto-update in running pods
✗ No audit trail of who read what
✗ YAML manifests can't be stored in Git without being a secret
```

sections.title: External Secrets Operator: syncing from a secret store
sections.body:
External Secrets Operator (ESO) reads secrets from an external store (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, etc.) and creates Kubernetes Secrets automatically. The sandbox uses ESO with a local secret store.

```
External Secret Store          ESO Operator          Kubernetes
(AWS Secrets Manager,    →    (controller)      →   Secret object
 GCP Secret Manager,          polls & syncs
 Vault, etc.)
```

**Key ESO objects:**

```yaml
# SecretStore — defines HOW to connect to the secret store
# (namespace-scoped; use ClusterSecretStore for cluster-wide)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secretsmanager
  namespace: production
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        secretRef:
          accessKeyIDSecretRef:
            name: aws-creds
            key: access-key-id
          secretAccessKeySecretRef:
            name: aws-creds
            key: secret-access-key
```

```yaml
# ExternalSecret — defines WHAT to sync
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: production
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h          # re-sync every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: db-credentials       # name of Kubernetes Secret to create
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: username      # key in Kubernetes Secret
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/db           # path in Secrets Manager
        property: username     # JSON field within the secret
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/db
        property: password
```

**Check ESO in the sandbox:**

```bash
# ESO is installed in the sandbox
kubectl get pods -n external-secrets
# Shows: external-secrets controller, cert-controller, webhook

# Check CRDs
kubectl get crds | grep external-secrets
# externalsecrets.external-secrets.io
# secretstores.external-secrets.io
# clustersecretstores.external-secrets.io

# View any configured ClusterSecretStores
kubectl get clustersecretstores

# View ExternalSecrets across all namespaces
kubectl get externalsecrets -A

# Check ESO sync status
kubectl describe externalsecret db-credentials -n production
# Status.Conditions shows if sync succeeded
```

**ESO with Vault:**

```yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault-backend
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: https://vault.example.com:8200
      path: secret
      version: v2
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: kubernetes
          role: my-app-role
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: external-secrets
            namespace: external-secrets
```

sections.title: HashiCorp Vault: full secret lifecycle management
sections.body:
HashiCorp Vault is the industry standard for secret management. It's an API-driven secret store with dynamic credentials, encryption as a service, and detailed audit logs.

**Vault concepts:**

```
Secret Engine   — backend that stores or generates secrets
                (kv-v2: key-value store, database: dynamic DB creds,
                 pki: certificate authority, aws: dynamic IAM creds)

Authentication  — how a client proves its identity
                (kubernetes: pod uses SA token, aws: IAM role,
                 ldap: corporate directory, approle: machine auth)

Policy          — what paths a token can access
                (path "secret/data/myapp/*" { capabilities = ["read"] })

Lease           — TTL on a secret (dynamic creds expire automatically)

Audit Device    — logs every request (file, syslog, socket)
```

**Core Vault operations:**

```bash norun
# Set Vault address and token
export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200
export VAULT_TOKEN=s.xyzABCdef123

# Write a secret
vault kv put secret/myapp/db \
  username=appuser \
  password=<CHANGE_ME>

# Read a secret
vault kv get secret/myapp/db
vault kv get -field=password secret/myapp/db

# List secrets at a path
vault kv list secret/myapp/

# Check your token's permissions
vault token lookup
vault token capabilities secret/myapp/db

# Dynamic database credentials (Vault generates them on-demand)
vault read database/creds/my-role
# Output: username=v-app-aB3xYz, password=A1b2C3d4..., lease_duration=1h
# → When TTL expires, credentials are revoked in the database automatically
```

**Vault Agent: auto-inject secrets into pods:**

```yaml
# Vault Agent Injector annotation-based injection
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  annotations:
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
    vault.hashicorp.com/role: "my-app-role"
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db.env: "secret/data/myapp/db"
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-db.env: |
      {{- with secret "secret/data/myapp/db" -}}
      export DB_USERNAME={{ .Data.data.username }}
      export DB_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.password }}
      {{- end }}
spec:
  serviceAccountName: my-app  # used for Vault k8s auth
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "source /vault/secrets/db.env && ./start.sh"]
```

**Sealed Secrets: encrypted secrets in Git:**

```bash norun
# Sealed Secrets controller runs in K8s, holds the private key
# kubeseal CLI encrypts secrets using the controller's public key

# Install kubeseal
curl -sSL https://github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets/releases/download/v0.24.5/kubeseal-0.24.5-linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
mv kubeseal /usr/local/bin/

# Create a sealed secret from a regular secret
kubectl create secret generic db-password \
  --from-literal=password=<CHANGE_ME> \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
  kubeseal --format=yaml > sealed-db-password.yaml

# The output is safe to commit to Git — only the controller can decrypt it
cat sealed-db-password.yaml
git add sealed-db-password.yaml && git commit -m "add sealed db password"

# ArgoCD syncs it → controller decrypts it → creates a real Secret
kubectl get secret db-password  # now exists as a regular Secret
```

sections.title: Exercise: explore ESO and secret patterns in the sandbox
sections.body:
The sandbox has External Secrets Operator installed. Explore how it works.

```bash
# ── 1. Inspect the ESO installation ──────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get pods -n external-secrets
kubectl get crds | grep external-secrets

# ── 2. Check what secret stores are configured ────────────────────────────
kubectl get clustersecretstores
kubectl get secretstores -A

# ── 3. Look at existing ExternalSecrets ───────────────────────────────────
kubectl get externalsecrets -A
if kubectl get externalsecret db-credentials -n learning 2>/dev/null; then
  kubectl describe externalsecret db-credentials -n learning
fi

# ── 4. Explore Kubernetes Secrets in the sandbox ──────────────────────────
# List all secrets (don't print values in a real system!)
kubectl get secrets -A | grep -v 'kubernetes.io/service-account'

# Look at the ArgoCD admin secret:
kubectl get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd -o yaml

# Decode it:
kubectl get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d && echo

# ── 5. Create a secret and consume it ────────────────────────────────────
kubectl create secret generic test-secret -n learning \
  --from-literal=api-key=my-super-secret-api-key \
  --from-literal=db-url=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb

# Verify it exists:
kubectl get secret test-secret -n learning -o yaml

# ── 6. Deploy a pod that reads the secret as env vars ─────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-consumer
  namespace: learning
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo API_KEY=$API_KEY && echo DB_URL=$DB_URL && sleep 60"]
    env:
    - name: API_KEY
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: test-secret
          key: api-key
    - name: DB_URL
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: test-secret
          key: db-url
  restartPolicy: Never
EOF

# Wait for it to start:
kubectl wait pod/secret-consumer -n learning --for=condition=ready --timeout=30s

# See the injected secrets:
kubectl logs secret-consumer -n learning

# ── 7. Secret rotation simulation ─────────────────────────────────────────
# Update the secret:
kubectl create secret generic test-secret -n learning \
  --from-literal=api-key=rotated-new-api-key \
  --from-literal=db-url=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Note: running pods do NOT automatically get the new value
# (env var injection is at pod start time)
# To pick up the new secret, the pod must be restarted
# (This is why mounted volume secrets or ESO with reloader is better)

# ── 8. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete pod secret-consumer -n learning
kubectl delete secret test-secret -n learning
```
